newsitem.title: MONACO: FEATURE - Royals seek lower profile at Monaco birthday bash.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Royals seek lower profile at Monaco birthday bash.

text.p: Monaco's royal family, which claims to be the longest-serving European royal dynasty, is hoping that its 700th anniversary will shift attention from its often steamy private lives to the principality's economic and cultural successes.

"I regret that Monaco's public image is so dependent on the princely family's popularity ratings," complained Prince Albert, who is being groomed by his father Prince Rainier III to rule the tiny state.

"I am prepared to believe that the family is interesting in the eyes of the media, but its private goings-on are too often lumped together with the country's every-day life," Albert, who is coordinating the anniversary celebrations, told the French daily Le Figaro in a rare interview.
It was on January 8, 1297, that Francois Grimaldi, disguised as a monk, sneaked into a Genoese-controlled fortress, let in his own soldiers and established the Grimaldi dynasty in what is now Monaco.

The principality, a sovereign state with less than two square km (one square mile) of territory nestling in the southeastern corner of France, kicks off 10 months of celebrations marking the founding of the dynasty with a gala next Wednesday (Jan 8).
Albert hopes the celebrations will be a showcase for Monaco's economic, humanitarian and environmental activities as well as its historic past.
So far, the focus has been mainly on his family's personal foibles.
IN THE MEDIA SPOTLIGHT
Monaco first came under the media spotlight when Prince Rainier married the glamorous American movie star Grace Kelly in 1956.
Three children later, media demand became insatiable for a glimpse of Rainier's stunning young family.

Initially the family seemed quite content to satisfy the needs of the ever-present paparazzi. Rainier, Grace and their children Caroline, Stephanie and Albert, became regular fixtures in the glossy photo magazines of the day.
But the family's luck turned sour in 1982 with Grace's death in a car crash.
The world avidly followed Princess Stephanie, now 31, through a series of failed career attempts as a fashion model, swimsuit designer and rock singer.

Her most recent appearance on magazine covers followed the publication in Italy of photographs of her ex-husband Daniel Ducruet, her former palace bodyguard, cavorting with "Miss Topless Belgium", Fily Houteman, by a pool at a French Riviera villa.
The couple, who have two children, were divorced in October, a few weeks after the pictures appeared.
Stephanie's older sister Caroline, aged 39, is believed to be the first princess to be photographed topless.
Her first marriage, to Parisian jet-setter Philippe Junot, 17 years her senior, ended after two years. Her second husband, Italian millionaire Stefano Casiraghi, died in a speedboat accident.
In her latest cover photos she is completely bald, a phenomenon she has not explained publicly, though she has willingly posed for pictures.

Prince Albert, slightly balding at 38, has not been as open with the press as his sisters but has nonetheless developed an image as a lady's man due to a long string of public appearances with the likes of Claudia Schiffer, Brooke Shields and Lisa-Marie Presley.
"Life will not be easy for my future wife," Albert told Le Figaro.

"I became accustomed at an early age to the incessant presence of photographers. Some of my girlfriends who have been exposed, even for a very brief time, to this sort of life were not at all pleased. This is one of the reasons I am not in a serious relationship at this time," he said.
White-haired Prince Rainier is 73 and had major heart surgery two years ago. But the prince, who has reigned since May 1949, seems in no hurry to turn his job over to Albert.
"I'm waiting for my son to feel ready to take over," he said in a recent interview.

"I don't want a brutal abdication. It must be done smoothly," he told the weekly Figaro Magazine. "In 1997, I will myself preside over the 700th anniversary of the arrival of the Grimaldi on the rock of Monaco."
MONACO'S ATTRACTIONS
Despite the family's personal turmoil, Monaco is by most accounts a sort of heaven on earth.
It is almost always sunny and crime and unemployment are virtually unknown.
Many of its 30,000 residents are wealthy stars, including Shirley Bassey, Ringo Starr and Boris Becker, drawn there by the principality's status as a tax haven.
Only French citizens must pay taxes, and the state, funded largely by the earnings of its casinos, has no debts.
Becoming a naturalised Monegasque requires personal approval by Prince Rainier. Only about 30 people a year get the nod.

Rainier has worked hard to transform Monaco from a playground for the rich into a diversified state with a broad-based economy. A recent building boom has left the landscape bristling with high-rise apartment blocks.

More than $200 million has been set aside for the 700th anniversary festivities which will include firework displays, sporting events, concerts, car races, plays, art exhibitions and a meeting of the International Whaling Commission.
Events planned for January 8 include a mass, the unveiling of a statue, a waterfront re-enactment of the principality's past glories and a concert by the Monte Carlo ballet and opera companies.
